q: Who founded the Stoic school of philosophy?
explain: Zeno of Citium founded the Stoic school in Athens around 300 BCE.
hook: Stoicism starts at Z-for-Zero: Zeno.

sources.title: Stoicism | Britannica
sources.quote: Stoicism is a school of Hellenistic philosophy founded by Zeno of Citium in Athens.

sources.title: Stoicism (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: The Stoic school was founded around 300 BCE by Zeno of Citium, a voracious reader of Socratic dialogues, who also studied under the Cynic Crates

q: The Stoics take their name from the Stoa Poikile; what does that name mean in English?
explain: Zeno taught in the Stoa Poikile (Painted Colonnade or painted porch) in Athens, which gave the school its name.
hook: Stoa = porch; Poikile = painted.

sources.title: Zeno of Citium | Britannica
sources.quote: Arriving at his own philosophy, he began to teach in the Stoa Poikile (Painted Colonnade), whence the name of his philosophy.

sources.title: Stoicism | Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy
sources.quote: The name comes from the Stoa Poikile, or painted porch, an open market in Athens where the original Stoics used to meet and teach philosophy.

q: Around what date was the Stoic school founded?
explain: Zeno founded the Stoa in Athens around 300 BCE, shortly after Epicurus founded his school there.
hook: Round number for a round porch: 300 BCE.

sources.title: Stoicism | Britannica
sources.quote: The Stoic school of philosophy was founded by Zeno of Citium around 300 BCE.

sources.title: Stoicism (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: The Stoic school was founded around 300 BCE by Zeno of Citium

q: Who succeeded Zeno of Citium as head of the Stoic school?
explain: Cleanthes of Assos headed the Stoa after Zeno's death, and was in turn succeeded by Chrysippus.
hook: Order of heads: Z, C, C (Zeno, Cleanthes, Chrysippus).

sources.title: Cleanthes | Britannica
sources.quote: Cleanthes (born 331/330 bc, Assos in the Troad, Asia Minor—died 232/231) was a Stoic philosopher who became head of the Stoic school (263–232 bc) after the death of Zeno of Citium.

sources.title: Stoicism (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: Zeno was succeeded in the leadership of the Stoa first by Cleanthes of Assos and then by Chrysippus of Soli

q: Which Stoic added 'with nature' to Zeno's formula for the goal of life, 'living in agreement'?
explain: Zeno defined the end as 'living in agreement'; his first successor Cleanthes made it 'living in agreement with nature'.
hook: Cleanthes cleaned up the formula: add nature.

sources.title: Stoicism (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: Cleanthes, [Zeno’s] first successor, added ‘with nature’, and represented it as follows: ‘the end is living in agreement with nature’.

sources.title: Marcus Aurelius (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: After Zeno, founder of the Stoa, lays down the goal (telos) as ‘living in agreement’, Cleanthes specifies ‘living in agreement with nature’

q: Which third head of the Stoa is regarded as the principal systematizer of Stoic philosophy?
explain: Chrysippus of Soli succeeded Cleanthes and is described as the Stoa's foremost theorist and systematizer.
hook: Chrysippus = the 'system' guy.

sources.title: Chrysippus | Britannica
sources.quote: Chrysippus (born c. 280 bc—died c. 206) was a Greek philosopher from Soli (Soloi) who was the principal systematizer of Stoic philosophy.

sources.title: Epictetus | Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy
sources.quote: of Chrysippus (c.290–207 B.C.E.) the extremely influential third head of the Stoa

q: Chrysippus came from which city?
explain: He is known as Chrysippus of Soli and headed the Stoa from around 230 until 206 BCE.
hook: Chrysippus stood solo at the top: Soli.

sources.title: Chrysippus | Britannica
sources.quote: Chrysippus (born c. 280 bc—died c. 206) was a Greek philosopher from Soli (Soloi)

sources.title: Stoicism (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: then by Chrysippus of Soli, who headed the school from around 230 until 206 BCE and was by all accounts its foremost theorist and systematizer.

q: Seneca served as tutor and adviser to which Roman emperor?
explain: Seneca became tutor to the future emperor Nero and was highly influential in the early years of Nero's reign.
hook: Seneca and Nero: the tutor and the tyrant.

sources.title: Seneca | Britannica
sources.quote: As Nero’s tutor, Seneca had considerable political influence in the early years of that emperor’s reign.

sources.title: Stoicism (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: a generation later Seneca served as advisor to Nero.

q: To which friend did Seneca address his Moral Letters?
explain: Seneca's Moral Letters to Lucilius (Epistulae morales) discuss a wide range of moral problems.
hook: Letters to Lucilius: L for Letters, L for Lucilius.

sources.title: Seneca | Britannica
sources.quote: Seneca wrote Stoic philosophical treatises, such as the Moral Letters to Lucilius, a series of essays which discuss a range of moral problems.

sources.title: Letters on Ethics: To Lucilius (University of Chicago Press)
sources.quote: Letters on Ethics includes vivid descriptions of town and country life in Nero’s Italy, discussions of poetry and oratory, and philosophical training for Seneca’s friend Lucilius.

q: How many letters make up Seneca's Moral Letters to Lucilius?
explain: The Moral Letters to Lucilius comprise 124 letters treating a range of moral problems.
hook: Think 1-2-4 letters to Lucilius.

sources.title: Moral Letters to Lucilius | Britannica
sources.quote: Ad Lucilium epistulae morales ( Moral Letters to Lucilius ). Those 124 brilliant essays treat a range of moral problems not easily reduced to a single formula.

sources.title: Letters on Ethics: To Lucilius (University of Chicago Press)
sources.quote: 123      Resisting external influences 124      The criterion for the human good Fragments of other letters

q: In what year did Seneca die?
explain: In 65 CE Seneca was accused of involvement in a conspiracy to murder Nero and was ordered to commit suicide.
hook: Seneca: sixty-five.

sources.title: Seneca | Britannica
sources.quote: In 65 Seneca’s enemies denounced him as having been a party to a conspiracy to murder Nero, and he was ordered to commit suicide.

sources.title: Seneca (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 1 BCE – CE 65) was born in Corduba (Spain) and educated—in rhetoric and philosophy—in Rome.

q: What was Epictetus's legal status as a boy?
explain: Epictetus was a slave as a boy, attended lectures by the Stoic Musonius Rufus, and later became a freedman.
hook: From chains to the most famous lessons on freedom.

sources.title: Epictetus | Britannica
sources.quote: As a boy he was a slave but managed to attend lectures by the Stoic Musonius Rufus. He later became a freedman

sources.title: Stoicism (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: Epictetus, a former slave, was expelled from Rome by Domitian along with other

q: Which pupil wrote down the teachings of Epictetus?
explain: Epictetus wrote nothing himself; his pupil Arrian transmitted his teachings in the Discourses and the Encheiridion.
hook: Arrian arranged Epictetus's words.

sources.title: Epictetus | Britannica
sources.quote: As far as is known, Epictetus wrote nothing. His teachings were transmitted by Arrian, his pupil, in two works: Discourses, of which four books are extant; and the Encheiridion, or Manual, a condensed aphoristic version of the main doctrines.

sources.title: Marcus Aurelius (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: Arrian, who wrote down Epictetus’ teachings, named them hupomnêmata

q: What is the Greek name of Epictetus's short 'Manual' or 'Handbook'?
explain: The Encheiridion, or Manual, is a condensed aphoristic version of Epictetus's main doctrines, compiled by Arrian.
hook: Enchiridion: a handbook small enough to keep 'in hand'.

sources.title: Epictetus | Britannica
sources.quote: the Encheiridion, or Manual, a condensed aphoristic version of the main doctrines.

sources.title: The Internet Classics Archive | The Enchiridion by Epictetus
sources.quote: The Enchiridion By Epictetus ... Translated by Elizabeth Carter

q: In which Greek city did Epictetus run his own school after leaving Rome?
explain: After his expulsion from Rome, Epictetus spent the rest of his life teaching at Nicopolis in Epirus, Greece.
hook: Nicopolis: a 'nice city' for a school.

sources.title: Epictetus | Britannica
sources.quote: The rest of his life Epictetus spent at Nicopolis.

sources.title: Epictetus | Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy
sources.quote: He lived and worked, first as a student in Rome, and then as a teacher with his own school in Nicopolis in Greece.

q: Which Roman emperor expelled Epictetus and other philosophers from Rome?
explain: In AD 90 Domitian expelled philosophers from Rome, irritated by Stoic sympathy for opponents of his tyranny.
hook: Domitian dominated, so the philosophers departed.

sources.title: Epictetus | Britannica
sources.quote: In ad 90 he was expelled from Rome with other philosophers by the emperor Domitian, who was irritated by the favourable reception given by Stoics to opponents of his tyranny.

sources.title: Stoicism (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: Epictetus, a former slave, was expelled from Rome by Domitian along with other

q: In Elizabeth Carter's translation, the Enchiridion opens: 'Some things are in our ___ and others not.' What is the missing word?
explain: This opening line is Epictetus's famous dichotomy of control: opinion, desire and aversion are in our control; body, property and reputation are not.
hook: Dichotomy of control: two piles, one word.

sources.title: The Internet Classics Archive | The Enchiridion by Epictetus
sources.quote: 1. Some things are in our control and others not. Things in our control are opinion, pursuit, desire, aversion, and, in a word, whatever are our own actions. Things not in our control are body, property, reputation, command, and, in one word, whatever are not our own actions.

sources.title: Stoicism | Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy
sources.quote: The starting point for Epictetus was the famous dichotomy of control, as expressed at the very beginning of the Enchiridion

q: Who wrote or taught: 'Men are disturbed, not by things, but by the principles and notions which they form concerning things'?
explain: This is section 5 of Epictetus's Enchiridion (Handbook), in Elizabeth Carter's translation.
hook: It's not the thing, it's your take on the thing: Epictetus.

sources.title: The Internet Classics Archive | The Enchiridion by Epictetus
sources.quote: 5. Men are disturbed, not by things, but by the principles and notions which they form concerning things.

sources.title: Aurelius, Marcus | Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy
sources.quote: As Epictetus put it, what upsets people are not things themselves but rather their judgements about things (see Handbook 5).

q: Which Roman emperor wrote the Meditations?
explain: The Meditations are Marcus Aurelius's Stoic reflections, probably written while on military campaign.
hook: Emperor by day, journaler by night.

sources.title: Marcus Aurelius | Britannica
sources.quote: Marcus Aurelius ... was a Roman emperor (161–180), best known for his Meditations on Stoic philosophy.

sources.title: Aurelius, Marcus | Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy
sources.quote: The philosophy of the Roman Emperor Marcus Aurelius can be found in a collection of personal writings known as the Meditations.

q: In what language did Marcus Aurelius write the Meditations?
explain: Though written by a Roman emperor, the Meditations were written in ancient Greek; the Greek manuscript title is ta eis heauton.
hook: A Roman thinking in Greek.

sources.title: Meditations | Britannica
sources.quote: Strikingly, though they comprise the innermost thoughts of a Roman, the Meditations were written in ancient Greek—to such an extent had the union of cultures become a reality.

sources.title: Aurelius, Marcus | Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy
sources.quote: The current Greek title— ta eis heauton (‘to himself’)—derives from a manuscript now lost and may be a later addition

q: What does the Greek manuscript title of Marcus Aurelius's Meditations, ta eis heauton, mean?
explain: The title Meditations is modern; the manuscripts carry ta eis heauton, 'to himself', which may not go back to Marcus himself.
hook: A diary addressed to its own author.

sources.title: Aurelius, Marcus | Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy
sources.quote: The current Greek title— ta eis heauton (‘to himself’)—derives from a manuscript now lost and may be a later addition (it is first recorded c. 900 by Arethas).

sources.title: Aurelius, Marcus, Meditations | Oxford Classical Dictionary
sources.quote: The title Meditations is purely modern: τά εἰς ἑαυτὸν (‘to himself’), found in our MSS, may not go back to the author, but is surely accurate.

q: According to the Stoics, what is the only true good?
explain: Stoics held that virtue is the only good, while things like wealth, health, and even life are indifferent.
hook: Only virtue is on the scoreboard.

sources.title: Stoicism | Britannica
sources.quote: Stoics believe that virtue is the only true good, and external factors like wealth, health, or life itself are indifferent.

sources.title: Stoicism (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: This sketch of Stoic eudaimonism allows us to better appreciate two of their most contentious ethical doctrines: (1) human happiness is fully in our power and (2) virtue is the only good.

q: The four cardinal virtues are wisdom, courage, justice and what?
explain: The Stoics recognized the four cardinal virtues of wisdom, courage, justice and temperance (moderation).
hook: W-C-J-T: Wise Courageous Just Temperate.

sources.title: Stoicism | Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy
sources.quote: the four cardinal virtues of wisdom, courage, justice and temperance, are the only good.

sources.title: Stoicism (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: The virtues – prudence, justice, courage, moderation and the rest – are good.

q: What did the Stoics call things such as health, wealth and reputation that are neither good nor bad?
explain: Things that neither benefit nor harm, like life, health and wealth, are indifferents; some are 'preferred' and may be pursued unless they compromise virtue.
hook: Nice to have, not needed to be good: indifferent.

sources.title: Stoicism (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
sources.quote: Everything which neither does benefit nor harms is neither of these: for instance, life, health, pleasure, beauty, strength, wealth, reputation, noble birth

sources.title: Stoicism | Internet Encyclopedia of Philosophy
sources.quote: Proēgmena = preferred indifferents, externals, outside of virtue that—other things being equal—can be pursued unless they compromise one’s virtue.

q: What does the Latin phrase 'amor fati' mean?
explain: Amor fati means love of fate: the welcoming of all life's experiences as good.
hook: Amor = love, fati = fate.

sources.title: AMOR FATI Definition & Meaning - Merriam-Webster
sources.quote: : love of fate : the welcoming of all life's experiences as good

q: What does the Latin phrase 'memento mori' literally mean?
explain: Memento mori is Latin for 'remember that you must die'; in English it names a reminder of mortality.
hook: Memento = remember; mori = to die.

sources.title: MEMENTO MORI Definition & Meaning - Merriam-Webster
sources.quote: Memento mori literally means "Remember you must die".

q: In the practice Cicero called praemeditatio futurorum malorum, what does one rehearse in advance?
explain: Praemeditatio futurorum malorum is the pre-rehearsal of future evils to soften their arrival; Cicero reports it from the Cyrenaics, and the Roman Stoics adopted it.
hook: Pre-meditate the bad so it can't ambush you.

sources.title: Appropriate Beliefs or Surrogate Satisfaction? Ancient Greek and Roman Perspectives on Imagining Future Evils (UCL)
sources.quote: For this reason, they recommended the practice of imaginative pre-rehearsal of future evils (praemeditatio futurorum malorum).

sources.title: Seneca philosophus - Bryn Mawr Classical Review
sources.quote: They propose the “premeditation of future evils” ( praemeditatio futurorum malorum ) to alert us to our daily problems and the principles with which to address them.
